name: Authoritarian capitalism
summary: Authoritarian capitalism is a regime type in which a market economy with mostly market-set prices and private and state firms runs under an authoritarian state: power is concentrated in a small elite, there is no independent legislature or judiciary, and speech, press, opposition and civil society are tightly controlled. The sources describe it as nationalist, integrated into the global economy, and hostile to liberal claims of universal values; Lee Kuan Yew's Singapore is its model case. The authoritarian neoliberalism strand (Edozie after Bruff) is the critical reading of the same pairing of market discipline with state power.
scope: A regime model in which a market economy with private property and market prices runs under an authoritarian state that restricts dissent and has no independent legislature or courts, as the defining scholarship and commentary describe it: Friedberg's 'nationalist authoritarian capitalism' of China and Russia (s1), Drezner on China's leaders' bid to loosen the economy while tightening politics (s2), Cassidy's account of Lee Kuan Yew's Singapore as its model (s3), John Lee's contrast of Chinese and Russian authoritarian capitalism with Western capitalism (s4), and Scheiring's account of Orbán's Hungary (s5). Its one named thinker is Lee Kuan Yew. The redirect 'authoritarian neoliberalism' is taken in Edozie's sense (s6, after Bruff): the neoliberal state insulated from democratic pressure, typified in Asia by the China model. Excluded: Deng Xiaoping's own Marxist-Leninist texts (his thought has its own profile, Deng Xiaoping Theory), Pinochetism, Putinism and other regime-specific ideologies, and Western liberal democracies as such. It is a regime type with commentators and a few defenders rather than a codified doctrine, so positions come from what those sources say the model holds.

sources.title: Uphold the Four Cardinal Principles (1979)

sources.usedFor: A Marxist-Leninist speech by the architect of China's reforms: Party leadership, socialist rather than bourgeois democracy, condemnation of disruptive protest; also its affirmation of class struggle and proletarian dictatorship. It does not discuss markets.

sources.title: The Authoritarian Challenge: China, Russia and the Threat to the Liberal International Order
sources.author: Aaron L. Friedberg (Sasakawa Peace Foundation, 2017)
sources.usedFor: Scholarly account of 'nationalist authoritarian capitalism' in China and Russia: concentrated power without independent legislatures or judiciaries, state capitalism with market prices, global integration, nationalism and patriotic education, surveillance, NGO and internet control, rejection of universal values.

sources.title: Can Authoritarian Capitalism Outlive Lee Kuan Yew?

sources.usedFor: Lee Kuan Yew's Singapore as the model of authoritarian capitalism and its influence on China.

sources.title: Western Vs. Authoritarian Capitalism
sources.author: John Lee, The Diplomat (2009)
sources.usedFor: The case for and against authoritarian capitalism as a rival to the Western model.

sources.title: Neoliberal democracy vs neoliberal authoritarianism: capitalism and democracy’s global contest in the twenty-first century (ch. 5 of Research Handbook on Democracy and Development)
sources.author: Rita Kiki Edozie, in Crawford and Abdulai (eds), Edward Elgar (2021)
sources.usedFor: Authoritarian neoliberalism after Bruff, typified in Asia by the China model.

abolish-hereditary-privilege.rationale: Meritocracy is rhetorically central, although elite families persist; weak agreement.

anonymous-payments.rationale: Scholars describe surveillance and control of the financial and digital sphere as core to these regimes.

assimilate-immigrants.rationale: China pursues assimilation while Singapore uses multiracial integration; split.

avoid-deficit-stimulus.rationale: Singapore is known for fiscal prudence and reserves, but China uses stimulus; adherents lean to prudence.

budget-needs-parliament.rationale: Parliaments approve budgets formally but are dominated by the leadership; split.

conscription.rationale: Singapore runs national service and China keeps conscription law, so adherents accept state power to conscript.

consent-of-governed.rationale: Lee said the government decides what is right regardless of popular opinion; legitimacy rests on performance rather than consent.

corporatist-bargaining.rationale: Singapore's tripartite NTUC arrangement is corporatist, but China and Russia differ, so adherents split.

correct-racial-injustice.rationale: The model favours merit and national stability over group-based remedies, though Singapore runs ethnic housing quotas for harmony; the evidence is indirect.

courts-bound-by-majority.rationale: The model rejects both constraint by courts and majority rule; split.

cultures-equal-different.rationale: Friedberg (introduction) says the regimes' nationalist narratives stress their own people's uniqueness and superior virtue.

decent-living-guarantee.rationale: Lee praised self-reliance and savings schemes over handouts but also defended a paternal state; adherents are divided on cutting welfare outright.

defeat-own-government-war.rationale: Nationalist loyalty to the state is central to the model as Friedberg describes it, so wishing one's own government defeated is rejected.

democracy-best.rationale: Cassidy reports Lee's argument, never abandoned, that Western-style democracy was not necessarily the best way to organise a country and that China's system would not end up like the American or British one.

direct-votes.rationale: Lee held that the government decides what is right regardless of popular opinion, so direct votes on laws are rejected.

discourage-race-mixing.rationale: Singapore promotes racial harmony and integration rather than discouraging mixing.

disparate-impact-discrimination.rationale: Merit selection is central; unequal outcomes are not discrimination.

diversity-weakens-cohesion.rationale: Singapore actively manages diversity for harmony, implying concern but not claiming diversity is a problem; split.

duties-before-rights.rationale: Friedberg (ch. 3, internal threats) says the regimes' ideologies stress the primacy of the collective, nation and state or nation and party, against liberalism's emphasis on individual freedom.

economy-in-majority-hands.rationale: Singapore is explicitly multiracial while Chinese and Russian nationalism favour the majority, so strands split and no stated position emerges.

educated-out-of-touch.rationale: The model relies on educated meritocratic officials and technocrats.

elective-rulers.rationale: Rulers are selected by party or tightly managed elections.

emergency-suspend-protections.rationale: Lee said in 1986 that Singapore has to lock people up without trial, and earlier denied that detention without charge is totalitarian.

end-racial-preferences.rationale: Singapore uses ethnic quotas in housing but stresses merit; split.

entrenched-bill-of-rights.rationale: These states have written constitutions with rights chapters, but Friedberg notes that they protect neither civil liberties nor basic rights in practice, and Lee held that the government decides what is right.

equal-outcomes.rationale: Meritocracy and unequal rewards drive Lee's model; equal outcomes are rejected.

ethnic-nation.rationale: Singapore built a multiracial policy and China an official multi-ethnic line, so adherents do not seek an ethnically pure nation.

every-country-ready-for-democracy.rationale: Cassidy reports Lee's argument, from which he never wavered, that Singapore and other Asian countries, China included, were not ready for Western-style democracy.

exit-over-voice.rationale: The model offers little voice, but Lee did not ground legitimacy in freedom of exit; the claim is a libertarian one that adherents do not adopt.

experts-over-public.rationale: Lee advocated rule by able, well-paid officials selected on merit and said the government decides what is right irrespective of public opinion.

family-wage.rationale: Lee Kuan Yew stressed family but favoured market wages and self-reliance; no stated position on a family wage.

flat-income-tax.rationale: Singapore's progressive but low rates mean no position; split.

foreign-land-ownership.rationale: China bars private ownership of land and Singapore allows some; split.

gender-parity-bodies.rationale: Merit selection is preferred over quotas.

harm-principle.rationale: Lee acknowledged interfering in citizens' private lives and defended it as necessary for economic progress, rejecting a limit of state action to harm prevention.

hereditarian-race.rationale: Lee made remarks on group traits, but the claim is not a core doctrine and adherents split.

history-own-civilization.rationale: Cultural-values and patriotic education fit the model.

institutions-fit-civilization.rationale: Cassidy reports Lee's view that Asian countries were not ready for Western-style democracy and would not end up with an American, British, French or German system.

land-use-tenure.rationale: Singapore state-owns land with leases and China has state land ownership; but adherents do not hold use-tenure as such; split.

mass-culture-pacifies.rationale: Adherents see mass media as a tool to reinforce values, not as pacification, and would deny this critical claim.

military-superiority.rationale: Friedberg (ch. 1, Origins) says the regimes' nationalist ideologies stress the need for military strength and constant vigilance against foreign aggression.

minority-language-support.rationale: Singapore supports four official languages while China pushes Mandarin; split.

moral-incentives.rationale: Lee argued that low salaries will not attract able men, showing reliance on material rewards; the model does not propose replacing them.

multipolar-world.rationale: Friedberg (ch. 2) records that both regimes wish to be recognised as poles in a multipolar world and cite the emergence of a multipolar system as desirable in official documents.

national-mission.rationale: Friedberg (introduction) states that, unlike their Cold War forebears, neither Russia's nor China's rulers see themselves as standard-bearers of a transnational creed they seek to spread.

natural-rulers.rationale: Lee argued for governing by an able elite chosen by merit and paid well; this is meritocratic rather than hereditary.

no-foreign-bases.rationale: Strands differ: China and Russia oppose foreign bases on principle while Singapore hosts allied facilities, so no single answer is supported.

nonpartisan-head-of-state.rationale: The head of state is typically the party leader in the model.

online-anonymity.rationale: Described as controlling the internet and NGOs and requiring state visibility into participants.

parliament-supreme.rationale: Parliament in Singapore is dominated by the executive party; split.

participatory-democracy.rationale: Concentrated power without independent legislatures and tight NGO control point against direct participation.

party-controls-media.rationale: Friedberg (ch. 1, Origins) names strict controls on speech and the press as a shared feature of the authoritarian capitalist regime type, and Cassidy notes Singapore sued or banned foreign publications.

patriotic-education.rationale: Friedberg describes China's Patriotic Education Campaign, launched in 1991, as the vehicle of the regime's new nationalist legitimacy.

people-in-arms.rationale: The state keeps a monopoly on arms.

person-over-state.rationale: Friedberg says the regimes' ideologies stress the primacy of the collective and impose strict controls on civil liberties and human rights, so they do not put individuals ahead of the state.

political-elite-corrupt.rationale: Lee's model claims to produce clean, efficient government through high pay and tough anti-corruption, so adherents deny that elites are corrupt in general.

population-transfer.rationale: Not an endorsed doctrine, though regimes have pressured minorities; low confidence.

preserve-national-culture.rationale: Friedberg (introduction and ch. 1) describes nationalist narratives drawing on the nation's unique history and culture as part of these regimes' official ideology.

priority-to-poor.rationale: Lee backed housing and savings for citizens but put growth and merit first; split.

promote-democracy-abroad.rationale: Friedberg (introduction and ch. 1) says these regimes see Western 'ideological evangelism' as a mortal threat, and John Lee notes Beijing and Moscow call the Western democratising agenda 'underhanded'.

promulgated-standing-laws.rationale: Friedberg describes concentrated power with no independent legislature or judiciary, so rulers act by discretion in practice, and Lee defended government by able men over rule bound by popular process.

public-service-media.rationale: The model controls the press and internet and treats media as an instrument of the state, so independent publicly funded media are rejected.

race-social-construct.rationale: The model has no race doctrine; Singapore's official multiracialism treats race as an administrative category while China's nationalism stresses Han ethnicity, so adherents split.

racial-segregation-law.rationale: Singapore enforces multiracial integration policy, opposing segregation by law.

reduce-immigration.rationale: Singapore actively imports labour and talent while China is closed to immigration; adherents are split and the sources are silent.

religious-nation.rationale: China and Singapore are officially secular or multi-faith; religious definition of the nation is not part of the model.

representatives-worker-pay.rationale: Lee argued that low salaries will not attract able men who succeed in the professions or business, so pay at an average worker's level is rejected.

restrict-hate-speech.rationale: The model restricts speech to protect social harmony and stability, so legal limits on hate speech fit, though the motive is order rather than anti-hate principle.

restrict-strikes-picketing.rationale: Lee said Singapore's unions are different and that British-style trade unionism would bankrupt the country, and he took a hard line on the 1980 pilots' strike; legal restriction of strikes follows.

right-to-buy-council-homes.rationale: Singapore's public housing is sold to citizens on long leases, giving broad ownership that adherents defend.

rule-by-example.rationale: Lee stressed honest, exemplary officials but also law and punishment; adherents split.

sacred-nation.rationale: Friedberg describes nationalism and patriotic education as pillars of the regimes, though calling the nation sacred is stronger than the sources say.

sacrifice-heritage.rationale: Preserving cultural values is a stated aim, so heritage should not be sacrificed.

security-forces-accountable.rationale: Lee defended detention without trial and the state's coercive powers, so legal accountability for past killings is opposed.

self-reliance-over-aid.rationale: Lee stressed self-reliance, although the models also attract foreign investment; mild agreement.

separated-powers.rationale: Friedberg (ch. 1, Origins) defines the regime type by decision-making power concentrated in a small elite unchecked by free elections, autonomous legislatures or independent judiciaries.

single-official-language.rationale: China promotes Mandarin while Singapore keeps four languages; split.

soldiers-refuse-war.rationale: Nationalism and patriotic education are core to the model, and the state expects obedience from its forces.

sovereign-above-law.rationale: The leadership is not bound by courts or constitutional limits in practice, as Lee said the government decides what is right.

state-as-business.rationale: Lee ran Singapore like a corporation with high official pay and efficiency, but citizens as customers who can leave is not his framing.

state-directs-investment.rationale: Friedberg (ch. 1, Origins) says the state in this regime type formulates plans, supports national champions, protects strategic sectors and shapes the economy's evolution, and John Lee notes state banks send most loans to state firms.

state-laws-apply-online.rationale: Friedberg (ch. 3) records the regimes' joint promotion of 'Internet sovereignty', under which every government claims the right to regulate internet use within its borders.

strong-leader.rationale: Friedberg (ch. 1, Origins) describes the regime type as ruled by vigorous, visible and popular 'maximum leaders' with power concentrated and unchecked by legislatures; John Lee reports admirers' envy of its ability to get things done.

suppress-opposition.rationale: Friedberg (ch. 1, Origins) lists strict controls on political opposition, civil society and NGOs among the shared features of authoritarian capitalist regimes, and Cassidy reports that Lee's Singapore routinely rounded up and imprisoned opponents.

surveillance-ok.rationale: Friedberg (ch. 3) records that both regimes expanded monitoring of electronic communication under the guise of fighting crime and preventing terrorism, and that surveillance is a standby of authoritarian regimes.

traditional-family.rationale: Lee called the family the building brick of society that endures while governments come and go.

unbreakable-encryption.rationale: The model subordinates liberties to security and surveillance, so encryption the state cannot break is opposed.

uniformed-youth.rationale: Singapore's national service and the state youth organisations of China and Russia show the model uses youth mobilisation, though it is not a defining feature.

unions-good.rationale: Lee accepted Singapore's own cooperative unions while rejecting adversarial British-style unionism, and the model tolerates only state-aligned labour bodies, so adherents value unions only on those terms.

universal-morality.rationale: Friedberg (ch. 1 and conclusion) records that these regimes reject Western claims of 'universal values' as subversive and build national belief systems in their place.

work-for-welfare.rationale: Lee emphasised self-reliance and work-based savings schemes over handouts.

workers-own-party.rationale: The model concentrates power without independent parties or legislatures; China bans independent workers' organisations and Lee ran one-party dominance.

missingStatements.text: Government officials should be paid market-level salaries so that able people are attracted and corruption is discouraged.
missingStatements.rationale: Lee argued that low salaries draw in hypocrites and fail to attract able men.
missingStatements.declined: Narrow administrative policy detail, not a defining position.

missingStatements.text: A government's legitimacy should rest mainly on its record of delivering prosperity and order rather than on elections.
missingStatements.rationale: Proponents argue rising living standards secure regime stability, and Lee said democracy has seldom brought good government to developing countries.

notes: Authoritarian capitalism is a regime label described mostly by commentators, so only features the defining sources present as common to the model are answered; positions on policy detail, religion, family, territory and welfare are null. Themes searched: government, economy, liberty, world, culture, globalism, technology. Lee Kuan Yew's own texts, Gat, Rudd and Carney could not be opened (see notFound), so Lee's views are taken through Cassidy. Deng Xiaoping's texts are not used (his thought has its own profile). Edozie's chapter (s6) treats authoritarian neoliberalism as a critique of the neoliberal state and supports no statement answer.

keyFigures.role: Singapore's long-time prime minister, whose authoritarian capitalism served as a model for China
keyFigures.quote: Lee Kuan Yew, the longtime leader of Singapore, who died on Monday at the age of ninety-two, didn’t have an “ism” attached to his name.
